title: Big Tech is betting $700 billion on AI. Healthcare will decide whether the bet pays off
key_facts: The column says Microsoft, Alphabet, Meta and Amazon are expected to spend more than $700 billion on capital expenditures this year on the infrastructure that supports AI.
US healthcare spending reached $5.3 trillion in 2024, or 18% of GDP; by some estimates close to $1 trillion goes to administration alone.
Demand for care continues to outpace the available clinical workforce, so time freed by AI could mean more patients seen rather than fewer staff.

Examples of big AI players moving into healthcare: Microsoft and Mayo Clinic are developing a frontier AI model for healthcare; Google Cloud and CVS Health have a long-term partnership to power CVS's Health100 platform with Gemini.

For 2026 the US Medicare administrator CMS applied a 2.5% efficiency adjustment to the work component of certain non-time-based physician services; Medicare already builds productivity into payment updates for hospitals, nursing facilities and home health.
The column argues providers that use AI early to cut documentation, intake or coordination costs capture savings before payment rates catch up.
It concludes healthcare 'may be one of the clearest places to find out' whether AI can produce productivity at a scale that justifies the investment.
quote_evidence: Microsoft, Alphabet, Meta and Amazon are expected to spend more than $700 billion on capital expenditures this year as they expand the infrastructure required to support AI.
U.S. healthcare spending reached $5.3 trillion in 2024, or 18% of GDP.
For 2026, CMS brought that logic to physician payment, applying a 2.5% efficiency adjustment to the work component of certain non-time-based services.
why_it_matters_hint: An argument that healthcare is the clearest test of whether AI spending pays off, with Medicare payment rules shaping how long providers keep any savings.
event_date: Fortune column dated 10 Oct 2026; no single event
notes: Opinion/commentary: Fortune's note says the opinions are the author's. The author is not named in the text read (the URL slug names Bill Miller and WellSky, not confirmed as authors). The piece gives no outcome data showing AI lowering care costs.
